About Behavior Analyst, Researcher and Digital Systems Designer. Juan Lopez studies how environments, information, and experiences affect people, then carries that understanding into clearer, more humane systems. A shared foundation Observation and implementation belong together. Behavior analysis is the primary lens through which I approach my work. It brings careful observation, consistent measurement, individual context, and socially meaningful outcomes into the same conversation. Rather than beginning with assumptions, I try to understand the conditions surrounding a person, a task, or a system before deciding what should change. My work in research, web development, e-commerce, and information design grows from that foundation. I build client websites with SitePad and WordPress, develop Shopify themes, and use Astro to create focused, lightweight websites. By shaping environments so that information is clearer, actions are easier to understand, and systems better support the people who use them. Across independent client projects, I have managed the full path from early strategy to launch. My work has included information architecture, visual design, development, responsive implementation, content structure, forms, business email, payment systems, and domain configuration. Each part of that process is guided by the same goal: create something practical without losing sight of the person on the other side of the screen. I am completing two bachelor’s degrees at Florida International University: Psychology on the Applied Behavior Analysis track, and Natural and Applied Sciences. My current credentials include Registered Behavior Technician certification through the Behavior Analyst Certification Board and Social and Behavioral Human Research training through the CITI Program. I also hold certifications in food safety management and agricultural studies, reflecting a broader foundation in responsible practice, applied science, and human-centered work. Research Questions designed to be tested I designed my Fall 2025 AI Misattribution study to examine how expectations about a source shape social evaluation. Using an online experiment, Qualtrics, and IBM SPSS, I kept the question focused, the conditions controlled, and the conclusions grounded in what the data could support. Client systems From early structure to launch I build websites for service businesses using SitePad, WordPress, and Astro, depending on what the project requires. My work can include information structure, responsive design, forms, business email, payments, domain configuration, content organization, and the final details needed to bring a complete website online. Commerce Storefronts with a clear direction Through World Cup Items and VX Nexus, I have developed Shopify themes, shaped visual direction, organized merchandising, configured commerce systems, and refined each storefront across screen sizes. I approach e-commerce as an environment that should make products easier to understand, compare, and act on without adding unnecessary pressure. Real-world experience Understanding people in motion. Working as a valet attendant has placed me in environments where
          trust, timing, communication, and attention matter immediately. Every
          shift requires me to observe what is happening, respond to changing
          conditions, and help people move through an experience with less
          uncertainty. Observation Coordination Responsibility Adaptation Live environment In motion 01 Arrival Read the entrance 02 Handoff Establish trust 03 Coordinate Adapt with the team 04 Return Complete the experience 01 Observation Reading the environment A busy entrance changes from one moment to the next. I pay attention to traffic, guest behavior, available space, team movement, and the small cues that signal what may be needed next. The work has taught me to look carefully before acting. 02 Trust Responsibility made visible People hand me something valuable and expect it to be handled with care. I build that trust through clear communication, consistency, attention to detail, and respect for each person’s circumstances. 03 Adaptation Staying clear under pressure Arrivals overlap, priorities shift, and unexpected problems appear quickly. I have learned to remain composed, coordinate with others, and adjust to changing conditions without losing sight of the person waiting in front of me. A system is not defined only by how it works under ideal conditions,
        but by how well it supports people when time, attention, and patience
        are already limited. Real conditions. Thoughtful responses.

Approach Evidence with humility. Structure with care. I study how environments and information affect what people can understand and accomplish. The goal is not to control people. It is to remove avoidable barriers and make choices easier to see. 01 Everyday language first Technical vocabulary is useful only when it makes the reasoning more precise. People should not need a glossary to understand the point. 02 Context matters A pattern is interpreted alongside the environment, the task, and the individual—not as a detached number. 03 Meaningful outcomes Measurement should return to what a person or team can do, understand, and choose in the real setting. ABA-Informed Design Pathway Five translations from research to practice. Each step connects an everyday need to a restrained behavioral concept and a practical design implication. 01 Stimulus salience and attending Make What Matters Easy to Notice Visual hierarchy, contrast, and placement make task-relevant information easier to distinguish from supporting detail. The most useful next action should stand out without competing unnecessarily for attention. Design implication: prioritize the next useful action, then layer in supporting detail. 02 Discriminative stimuli Use Clear Cues for Action Labels, controls, and interface states should signal which actions are available and which are likely to work. Consistent cues reduce guesswork and help people move through a system with greater confidence. Design implication: use stable labels, recognizable controls, and predictable states. 03 Task analysis, prompting, and fading Support Progress in Manageable Steps Complex tasks become more approachable when they are divided into meaningful steps and supported at the moment help is needed. That assistance should gradually recede as the person becomes more capable of completing the task independently. Design implication: sequence difficult tasks, provide timely guidance, and fade support when it is no longer needed. 04 Consequences and reinforcement Make Outcomes Clear and Consistent Immediate, accurate feedback helps people determine whether an action worked. A consequence functions as reinforcement only when it makes the behavior it follows more likely to occur again. Design implication: confirm outcomes, preserve progress, and make effective actions easy to repeat. 05 Social validity and data-based decisions Measure Meaningful Outcomes A useful system should be evaluated by outcomes that matter to the people using it. Measure whether important tasks become more successful, efficient, or independent, identify barriers, and revise the environment when results fall short. Design implication: define observable success with users and let the results guide refinement. Ethical foundation Autonomy and dignity are part of the method. Behavior analysis is strongest when socially meaningful goals, informed choice, compassion, and respect are treated as requirements. In digital work, that means avoiding deceptive pressure, making outcomes understandable, and allowing people to change their minds. Primary sources Wolf (1978): social validity Stimulus control research and practice Prompting and fading research BACB Ethics Code for Behavior Analysts Baer, Wolf, and Risley: dimensions revisited

Research Questions before conclusions. Research helps me separate an intuition from evidence. The public summaries here keep methods, findings, and limits close together. Fall 2025 Academic Research AI (Mis)attribution: Perceiver Expectations About Agent Origin as a Driver of Social Evaluations in Text-Based Interactions An online experiment asking whether people judge the same interaction differently when they believe artificial intelligence is involved. Main finding: Participants rated the conversation as more natural when they believed both speakers were human, even though the transcript was unchanged. Read the research summary Same transcript ~446 words H–H Human–Human H–AI Human–AI AI–AI AI–AI Course FIU Research Methods II Author Juan D. Lopez Sample N = 123 in Study One Tools Qualtrics · IBM SPSS

Research · Fall 2025 AI (Mis)attribution AI (Mis)attribution: Perceiver Expectations About Agent Origin as a Driver of Social Evaluations in Text-Based Interactions Academic Research Research question Does the label change the judgment? An online experiment asking whether people judge the same interaction differently when they believe artificial intelligence is involved. Qualtrics IBM SPSS Online study Sample N = 123 Conditions Three Transcript Identical Same transcript ~446 words H–H Human–Human H–AI Human–AI AI–AI AI–AI Author Juan D. Lopez Course FIU Research Methods II Term Fall 2025 Last reviewed July 26, 2026 Administration Online Sample N = 123 in Study One Tools Qualtrics and IBM SPSS Methods Online between-subjects experiment, Identical transcript control, Six-point evaluation scales Conditions Human–Human, Human–AI, AI–AI Discuss the research Short answer What did the study find? Participants rated the conversation as more natural when they believed both speakers were human, even though the transcript was unchanged. This online course study was last reviewed on July 26, 2026 . The interpretation and limitations below apply to this study's specific text-based setting. Research question Do people judge the same interaction differently when they believe artificial intelligence is involved? Theoretical background People interpret a message alongside beliefs about its source. Research on agency, social evaluation, and human–AI interaction suggests that labels can shape expectations before a conversation is evaluated. Hypotheses Study One predicted that origin labels would influence naturalness, humanness, and thoughtfulness ratings. The warm-versus-cold extension tested whether tone would alter evaluations differently for human-labeled and AI-labeled responses. Study One design The study was conducted online. One hundred twenty-three participants were assigned equally to Human–Human, Human–AI, or AI–AI conditions. Each person evaluated the same approximately 446-word transcript. Only the stated origin of the speakers changed. Questionnaire and participant materials were created in Qualtrics. Data were analyzed in IBM SPSS. Main finding Naturalness differed across the three label conditions, F (2, 120) = 8.05, p < .001. The Human–Human condition received higher ratings than Human–AI and AI–AI. The two AI-involved labels did not differ significantly from each other. This supports a bounded conclusion: in this study, the label surrounding the exchange affected how the unchanged conversation was evaluated. Proposed and completed extension The second study crossed responder identity with warm or cold tone. The strongest pattern was that warmth improved evaluations of a human-labeled response, while the same tone contrast did not change evaluations of an AI-labeled response in the same way. Limitations The research used convenience university samples and one text-based academic context. Those limits matter. The results should not be generalized to all people, all AI systems, or all forms of conversation. Reflection The study made context impossible to ignore. People were not only responding to words; they were responding to what they believed those words represented. Method at a glance The control was the conversation itself. Held constant The same approximately 446-word transcript The online evaluation flow The response scales Changed The stated origin of the two speakers Human–Human, Human–AI, or AI–AI label Available evidence What can—and cannot—be claimed. Available outcomes Study One found higher naturalness ratings in the Human–Human condition than in either condition labeled as involving AI Limitations Convenience university sample Single text-based academic interaction Results should not be generalized to every AI interaction Responsible interpretation A difference in this setting, not a universal rule. The findings show that origin beliefs affected social evaluation in the study's text-based context. They do not establish that all people reject AI, that labels always dominate content, or that any system can control judgment.
